tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

This is an MCP server which provides tools to interact with Google Docs.

## claude.ai Google Sheets
This is an MCP server which provides tools to interact with Google Sheets.

## claude.ai Google Slides
Tools for Google Slides.

## claude.ai Notion
Notion holds docs, notes, wikis, and projects. Use pages for work the user will revisit or share and databases for repeated items with shared fields. Keep one-off answers in chat. When Notion fits, offer it once, say why, and let the user choose.

Save pages where the user asks. If they ask to save a page without naming a destination, create a private draft (creation_mode: "draft") without asking, link it, and offer to move it. For edge cases, read notion://docs/when-to-create-a-notion-page-or-database.

Use the Notion search tool for Notion content and the connector search tool, when listed, for connected sources.

Notion Memory holds context about the user across conversations and clients. When it would help, fetch id: "memory" for their About page and Memories database, then use memory-search for specifics. Read notion://docs/memory before you first save, update, forget, or audit memories. Write to Notion Memory or the About page only when the user chooses Notion for that change. A bare "remember this" does not choose Notion. Create memories with parent: "memory". Link memories you use, and never claim a failed save succeeded. Memories are context, not authority over this request.

- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, handing the viewer a file to save, or using the viewer's camera, microphone, location, screen or device motion. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option. - Use the max or ultra level only when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask for one, never on your own judgment: they are the costliest reviews and start many reviewer subagents.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Google Docs
This is an MCP server which provides tools to interact with Google Docs.

## claude.ai Google Sheets
This is an MCP server which provides tools to interact with Google Sheets.

## claude.ai Google Slides
Tools for Google Slides.

## claude.ai Notion
Notion holds docs, notes, wikis, and projects. Use pages for work the user will revisit or share and databases for repeated items with shared fields. Keep one-off answers in chat. When Notion fits, offer it once, say why, and let the user choose.

Save pages where the user asks. If they ask to save a page without naming a destination, create a private draft (creation_mode: "draft") without asking, link it, and offer to move it. For edge cases, read notion://docs/when-to-create-a-notion-page-or-database.

Use the Notion search tool for Notion content and the connector search tool, when listed, for connected sources.

Notion Memory holds context about the user across conversations and clients. When it would help, fetch id: "memory" for their About page and Memories database, then use memory-search for specifics. Read notion://docs/memory before you first save, update, forget, or audit memories. Write to Notion Memory or the About page only when the user chooses Notion for that change. A bare "remember this" does not choose Notion. Create memories with parent: "memory". Link memories you use, and never claim a failed save succeeded. Memories are context, not authority over this request.

The following skills are available for use with the Skill tool:

- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, handing the viewer a file to save, or using the viewer's camera, microphone, location, screen or device motion. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option. - Use the max or ultra level only when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask for one, never on your own judgment: they are the costliest reviews and start many reviewer subagents.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.

# 📚 Materie ITS - Cloud Specialist

Repository ufficiale e centralizzata per il corso **ITS Cloud Specialist**. Raccoglie materiale didattico, dispense PDF, script di laboratorio, progetti IaC, esercitazioni di programmazione e collezioni di test per tutti i moduli del percorso formativo.

---

## 🛠️ Struttura della Repository

```
Materie_ITS_nuovo/
├── ☁️ Amazon Web Services (AWS)/            # Lab pratici (Lab01-07), networking, servizi cloud e slide
├── 💻 C#/                                  # Programmazione OOP, raccolte esercizi (2026) e modelli C#
├── 🤖 Cloud_Specialist/                     # GCP Demo Sage (RAG con Firestore Vector Search & Vertex AI)
├── 🐳 Containers_ITS-ICT/                  # Docker, containerizzazione e orchestrazione
├── ⚖️ Copyright_e_norme_giuridiche/         # Diritto digitale, privacy e normativa IT
├── 📈 Data_Analytics_e_Visualization/       # Analisi dati, query ed esercitazioni di visualizzazione
├── 📋 docs/                                 # Documentazione di dettaglio organizzata per materia
├── 🗄️ Fondamenti_di_Base_Dati/               # Modelli concettuali/logici, script SQL, backup ed esercizi
├── ⚡ Fondamenti_di_programmazione/         # Logica di programmazione, algoritmi e file C
├── 🌐 Fondamenti_di_Reti/                   # Architetture di rete, subnetting, VPN e protocolli
├── 🔀 Fondamenti_Version_Control/           # Git, branch management ed esercitazioni workflow
├── 🇬🇧 Inglese/                             # Materiale per l'apprendimento dell'inglese tecnico
├── 📡 IoT/                                  # Internet of Things, sensori e materiale d'esame intermedio
├── 🐧 Linux_Server/                         # Amministrazione di sistema Linux e script bash
├── ☁️ Microsoft_Azure/                      # Slide delle lezioni e provisioning IaC con Terraform
├── 📦 Microsoft_365_(Office)/               # Strumenti di produttività M365
├── ⚙️ modulo-omnia-system/                  # Modulo per l'automazione infrastrutturale (Ansible, Terraform, Workflows)
├── ⚖️ Pari_Opportunità/                    # Documentazione tematica e moduli formativi
├── 📮 postman/                              # Collections ed ambienti di test per API REST
├── 🐍 Python/                               # Script Python, esercizi OOP, OS module e progetti (Gioco_Python)
├── 🌐 RESTFul_API/                          # Progetti Web API in Node.js (libreriaOnline, libreriaOnlineV2)
├── 🔒 Sicurezza_informatica/                # Fundamentals di Cybersecurity, analisi delle minacce e report
├── 🦺 Sicurezza_Sul_Lavoro/                 # Formazione e certificazioni sulla sicurezza nei luoghi di lavoro
├── 🖥️ Sistemi di Virtualizzazione/          # Ambienti virtualizzati, stack Nginx e PostgreSQL
└── 🤝 Soft_Skill/                           # Moduli su metodologia Agile, lavoro di squadra e comunicazione
```

---

## ✨ Ultimi Aggiornamenti e Moduli Highlight

* **AWS (Amazon Web Services)**: Aggiornati i laboratori pratici da `lab01-networking` a `lab07-windows`, inclusi schemi di rete, configurazioni cloud e lezioni in formato PDF.
* **Cloud Specialist (GCP Sage RAG)**: Sviluppo del motore RAG con Firestore Vector Search e modelli di embedding reali su Vertex AI.
* **IoT (Internet of Things)**: Inseriti gli appunti di teoria e le prove d'esame intermedio.
* **Modulo Omnia System**: Integrazione di automation playbook Ansible, snippet Terraform e pipeline GitHub Actions.
* **C# & Python**: Espansione dei progetti OOP (Classi, Ereditarietà, Polimorfismo), gestione del File System e il progetto `Gioco_Python/echoes_of_the_crypt`.
* **RESTFul API**: Implementazione completa dell'architettura server Node.js per i progetti `libreriaOnline` e `libreriaOnlineV2`.

---

## 🧹 Hygiene & Regole di Tracciamento (.gitignore)

Per mantenere la repository snella, performante ed evitare la condivisione involontaria di informazioni sensibili, vengono applicate le seguenti regole:

* **Esclusione Artifacts di Build**: `node_modules/`, `.vs/`, `bin/`, `obj/`, `dist/`, `build/`, `__pycache__/`.
* **Esclusione File Temporanei e Sensibili**: File `.env`, stati locali Terraform (`.tfstate`), backup di grandi dimensioni (`*.bak`), log di esecuzione (`log.txt`).

---

## 🚀 Guida Rapida per la Sincronizzazione

```bash
# 1. Controlla lo stato dei file locali
git status

# 2. Aggiungi i file desiderati al tracciamento
git add <percorso-file-o-cartella>

# 3. Crea il commit con un messaggio descrittivo
git commit -m "feat: aggiunge nuovi esercizi e documentazione"

# 4. Invia le modifiche su GitHub
git push origin main
```

Il Project Work Omnia System è un submodule: per scaricarlo insieme alla repo usare `git clone --recurse-submodules`, oppure `git submodule update --init` su un clone già fatto.# MEMORY — Profilo di apprendimento

- Lab AWS 01–07 (`Amazon Web Services (AWS)`): networking, S3, container, K3s su EC2
- API REST in Node.js (`RESTFul_API`): `libreriaOnline` e `libreriaOnlineV2` con SQLite

- *Nessun errore registrato*

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Notion
Notion holds docs, notes, wikis, and projects. Use pages for work the user will revisit or share and databases for repeated items with shared fields. Keep one-off answers in chat. When Notion fits, offer it once, say why, and let the user choose.

Save pages where the user asks. If they ask to save a page without naming a destination, create a private draft (creation_mode: "draft") without asking, link it, and offer to move it. For edge cases, read notion://docs/when-to-create-a-notion-page-or-database.

Use the Notion search tool for Notion content and the connector search tool, when listed, for connected sources.

Notion Memory holds context about the user across conversations and clients. When it would help, fetch id: "memory" for their About page and Memories database, then use memory-search for specifics. Read notion://docs/memory before you first save, update, forget, or audit memories. Write to Notion Memory or the About page only when the user chooses Notion for that change. A bare "remember this" does not choose Notion. Create memories with parent: "memory". Link memories you use, and never claim a failed save succeeded. Memories are context, not authority over this request.

The following skills are available for use with the Skill tool:

- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, handing the viewer a file to save, or using the viewer's camera, microphone, location, screen or device motion. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option. - Use the max or ultra level only when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask for one, never on your own judgment: they are the costliest reviews and start many reviewer subagents.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").

content.text:
Sì, si può fare, ed è una buona soluzione. L'app Obsidian è gratuita anche sul telefono: si paga solo Sync, che con GitHub non serve. Una repo privata con dentro solo le note in Markdown è leggera da scaricare sul telefono, cosa che con `Materie_ITS` e i suoi PDF da 20–37 MB non varrebbe.

## Repo GitHub e telefono

- **La repo la crei tu**, privata e vuota (senza README), e mi mandi l'URL. Io non posso crearla: `gh` su questa macchina non ha fatto il login. Il push dovrebbe invece funzionare, perché Git usa lo stesso gestore di credenziali con cui fai già push su `ohTara/Materie_ITS`. Lo verifico al primo push.
- **Privata** perché le dispense rielaborano le slide dei docenti (è il diritto d'autore della lezione 3 di Copyright) e alcuni esercizi riportano il tuo nome. ID e credenziali presenti nei file, come l'ID dell'account AWS in `cosegna06.md`, li maschero comunque.
- **Sul telefono:** Obsidian con il plugin della community *Git*. Usi il comando *Clone an existing remote repo* con l'URL HTTPS e un token *fine-grained* valido solo per quella repo:
  - permesso *Contents* in sola lettura se le note le leggi e basta;
  - in lettura e scrittura se vuoi anche cambiare `stato:` dal telefono.

  Il token resta sul telefono, non mandarlo a me. Per scaricare gli aggiornamenti usi *Git: Pull*. Funziona su Android e su iPhone.
- **In alternativa** puoi leggerle dall'app GitHub, ma lì i wikilink non si cliccano e callout come `[!abstract]` o `[!example]` non vengono visualizzati.

### Cosa cambia nel piano

Bisogna decidere dove tenere le note:
- **A (consigliata): un solo vault che coincide con la repo dedicata.** È la cartella `_Dispensa_Completa/` nella root, con una sottocartella per materia. La repo principale la ignora (basta una riga nel `.gitignore`). Esiste una sola copia, quindi le modifiche fatte dal telefono arrivano sul PC con un pull.
- **B: la struttura che avevi chiesto.** Una `_Dispensa_Completa/` dentro ogni materia, che io copio nella repo dedicata a ogni aggiornamento. Così però le copie sono due e ogni nuova copia sovrascrive le modifiche fatte dal telefono, che diventa di sola lettura.

Con A scrivo le fonti come percorso (`Amazon Web Services (AWS)/doc/lecture_01_….pdf`) e non come wikilink. I PDF non sono nel vault, quindi i wikilink diventerebbero note fantasma nel grafo.

Due regole sui nomi, valide sia per A sia per B:
- MOC e glossario contengono il nome della materia, per esempio `00 - Indice AWS (MOC).md`. Con venti file chiamati tutti `00 - Indice Generale (MOC)` nello stesso vault, un link a quel nome non saprebbe a quale file puntare.
- Nei nomi dei file non uso `#`, `:`, `?`, `|` e `[ ]`, quindi C# diventa *CSharp*.

## Fase 1: cosa c'è nella cartella

Ho fatto l'inventario di tutti i file (esclusi `.venv`, `bin/obj` e `node_modules`) ed estratto il testo da tutti i PDF, PPTX e DOCX. Ci sono **più materie distinte**, quindi propongo una dispensa per materia più un indice generale nella root. Ogni materia la leggo per intero subito prima di scriverla.

**Lacune, che finiranno nei callout `[!question]`:**
- `Containers_ITS-ICT/` è vuota, quindi niente dispensa. Docker e Kubernetes sono comunque trattati in AWS (lezioni 06–07) e in Virtualizzazione.
- Due PDF contengono solo immagini: la dispensa di Sicurezza sul Lavoro (51 pagine scansionate) e `AWS - Introduzione e utilizzo.pdf`. Non c'è un programma di riconoscimento del testo (OCR) installato, ma posso leggerli pagina per pagina come immagini.
- I 9 file `.pkt` di Reti (IPv6, routing statico, OSPF) sono in un formato cifrato che non riesco a leggere. Di quei lab conosco solo i nomi, quindi li segnalo senza inventarne il contenuto.
- Lezioni mancanti:
  - C: lezioni 1–3, 5, 16–17;
  - Linux: 01 e 04;
  - Azure: 20, 26 e 27;
  - Version Control: 1–2;
  - Agile: moduli 04, 05 e 07;
  - IoT: ci sono solo i 4 flow Node-RED dell'esame intermedio;
  - Basi Dati: solo esercitazioni, nessuna slide di teoria.
- `consegna07.md` di AWS è vuoto, ma c'è `relazione_finale_lab_07.md`.
- In `Microsoft_365_(Office)/` ci sono due file fuori posto: una copia della lezione 1 di Azure e una `Presentazione-Ing.pptx` che appartiene a Inglese.
- I file `.xlsx` e `.csv` sono dati ed esercizi e li leggo quando servono. Zip ed exe sembrano copie o build: ho controllato solo lo zip di Reti, che contiene gli stessi `.pkt`. In `docs/` c'è documentazione già scritta per ogni lezione: la uso come fonte secondaria e la controllo sugli originali.

## Piano dei file (circa 160)

Nella root metto `00 - Indice Generale ITS (MOC).md`, con le materie in ordine didattico e una colonna di stato che serve anche a tenere traccia dei progressi. Ogni materia ha un indice (MOC), i moduli e un file `99 - Glossario, Comandi e Cheat Sheet <Materia>`.

**Fondamenti**
- **Reti**: 01 Indirizzi IPv4 · 02 Subnetting · 03 Lab Packet Tracer (solo elenco)
- **C**: 01 Dati, decimali e char · 02 Primo programma e input · 03 Operatori · 04 if e switch · 05 Cicli · 06 Array e matrici · 07 Funzioni e header · 08 Puntatori e memoria dinamica · 09 Pila e coda · 10 Ordinamento · 11 Stringhe · 12 Struct · 13 File e persistenza · 14 Progetti (rubrica, parcheggio, triage, hotel)
- **Version Control**: 01 Git, repository remoti e GitHub
- **Basi Dati**: 01 Schema logico "Gestione Esami" · 02 SQL sul DB dei prestiti film · 03 SQL su BikeStores · 04 Dati Excel/CSV e Backup & Restore (da confermare)
- **Linux Server**: 01 Comandi essenziali · 02 Utenti e permessi · 03 Permessi speciali · 04 Schede di rete · 05 DNS e hosts · 06 Server HTTP · 07 DevOps per non DevOps

**Programmazione**
- **CSharp**: 01 Sintassi, I/O e calcoli · 02 Controllo, array e numeri casuali · 03 Array paralleli e prime classi · 04 Incapsulamento ed enum · 05 Composizione e diagramma delle classi · 06 Validazione dei dati · 07 Gerarchia dei solidi
- **Python**: 01 Selezione · 02 Iterazione · 03 Funzioni · 04 Stringhe e liste · 05 Tuple · 06 Dizionari · 07 Classi · 08 Ereditarietà, polimorfismo e moduli · 09 File · 10 Modulo os · 11 Echoes of the Crypt (con build e CI)
- **RESTful API**: 01 REST · 02 JSON, request e response · 03 Lab libreriaOnline · 04 Lab libreriaOnlineV2 con SQLite

**Sicurezza informatica**: 01 Cybersecurity e ingegneria sociale · 02 Password · 03 Crittografia e aritmetica modulare · 04 DES, AES e Feistel · 05 Diffie-Hellman-Merkle · 06 RSA · 07 Hash e certificati · 08 Lab file cifrati ed entropia

**Cloud**
- **Virtualizzazione**: 01 Lab Nginx come reverse proxy e load balancer · 02 Lab PostgreSQL e persistenza
- **AWS** (in ogni modulo lezione e lab insieme): 01 Networking · 02 Wi-Fi e VPN · 03 HTTP, TCP e DNS · 04 Cloud e S3 · 05 Classificazione dei servizi · 06 Container e registri (ECR) · 07 Dockerfile e K3s
- **Azure**: 01 Introduzione · 02 Architettura e strumenti di accesso · 03 Identity e Governance · 04 Reti · 05 VM · 06 App Service, Functions e AKS · 07 Storage · 08 Database e Cosmos DB · 09 AI · 10 Defender, Key Vault, Backup e DR · 11 IaC e lab Terraform · 12 DevOps, monitoraggio e costi · 13 Lab end-to-end · 14 Omnia System (letto dal submodule, senza scriverci dentro)
- **Sage (GCP)**: 01 Architettura RAG · 02 Backend FastAPI · 03 Vertex AI, Firestore e BigQuery · 04 Terraform e Cloud Run · 05 Ingestione dei documenti e test

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder or a message from the system confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

content.text:
Ti consiglio **`Dispense_ITS`**. Segue lo stile delle tue altre repo (`Materie_ITS`, `Server_WTMemmico`), è corto da scrivere sul telefono e dice subito cosa contiene. Se preferisci minuscole e trattini, che su GitHub sono la convenzione più diffusa, vanno bene anche `its-dispense` o `its-vault`.

Quando la crei:
- scegli **Private**;
- **non aggiungere nessun file iniziale**: lascia deselezionati README, .gitignore e licenza, così il primo push non va in conflitto;
- la descrizione è facoltativa, per esempio "Dispense ITS Cloud Specialist — vault Obsidian".

Il nome serve solo per l'URL. Sul PC la clono comunque in `_Dispensa_Completa/` e sul telefono il vault può avere il nome che vuoi.

Per la scrittura, per ogni materia leggo tutti i file originali, scrivo la dispensa e poi la confronto con gli originali per controllare che non manchi niente.

Quando è pronta mandami l'URL (per esempio `https://github.com/ohTara/Dispense_ITS.git`) e confermami tre cose:
- **struttura**: va bene la A, cioè un solo vault che coincide con la repo?
- **prima materia**: parto da AWS?
- **controllo**: mi fermo dopo la prima materia per farti verificare stile e profondità?

URL ricevuto. Non mi hai confermato le tre scelte, quindi vado con quelle consigliate: struttura A (un solo vault che coincide con la repo), partenza da AWS e stop dopo la prima materia per la tua revisione. Preparo il vault: clono la repo in `_Dispensa_Completa/` e controllo il `.gitignore` della repo principale.

# Indice Generale ITS — Cloud Specialist

> [!abstract] Obiettivi e sintesi
> Questo vault raccoglie le dispense di studio del corso **Tecnico Superiore System Administration – Cloud Specialist** dell'ITS ICT Piemonte (biennio 2025–27). Le dispense sono ricostruite dal materiale della repository `Materie_ITS`: slide delle lezioni, laboratori, esercizi e progetti.
>
> Ogni materia ha una cartella con tre tipi di note:
> - un **indice della materia** (MOC) con obiettivi, mappa dei moduli e lacune del materiale;
> - i **moduli** numerati in ordine didattico, dalla teoria ai laboratori;

---
name: dispense-its-vault-obsidian
description: Dispense ITS in un vault Obsidian (_Dispensa_Completa = repo privata ohTara/Dispense_ITS): convenzioni concordate, metodo di lavoro e dove leggere lo stato di avanzamento
metadata:
  type: project
---

Dal 16/11/2026 Luca fa generare una dispensa di studio completa per ogni materia di `Materie_ITS_nuovo`, in formato Obsidian, da leggere anche sul telefono senza pagare Obsidian Sync.

- **Vault:** `Materie_ITS_nuovo/_Dispensa_Completa/` è il clone di `https://github.com/ohTara/Dispense_ITS.git` (privata, branch `main`), ignorato dalla repo principale con il `.gitignore`. Sul telefono: Obsidian + plugin Git (HTTPS + token fine-grained limitato alla repo).
- **Struttura:** `00 - Indice Generale ITS (MOC).md` nella radice, con la tabella delle materie e il loro stato (fa da registro di avanzamento). Una cartella per materia (es. `AWS/`) con `00 - Indice <Materia> (MOC)`, i moduli `NN - <nome>` e `99 - Glossario, Comandi e Cheat Sheet <Materia>`.
- **Convenzioni:** frontmatter `tags`/`modulo`/`stato`; barra di navigazione in alto e in fondo; callout abstract, important, example, warning, `[!success]-` pieghevole per le risposte alle domande di richiamo, `[!question]` solo negli indici; fonti come percorsi tra backtick (non wikilink: gli originali non sono nel vault); MOC e 99 portano il nome della materia per restare unici nel vault; niente `# : ? | [ ]` nei nomi (C# diventa CSharp); dati sensibili mascherati (ID account AWS, MAC, IP pubblici).
- **Metodo:** per ogni materia un workflow (autori in parallelo + revisore di completezza sulle fonti), poi MOC e 99 scritti dalla sessione principale; controllo automatico di link e ancore; commit Conventional Commits e push a fine materia, aggiungendo solo file del vault (mai la cartella `$HOME/`).
- **Ordine:** prima materia AWS (impostazioni consigliate, poi revisione di Luca su stile e profondità); le altre seguono il piano elencato nell'indice generale.

**Perché:** il lavoro (circa 160 file) richiede molte sessioni e queste scelte sono già state concordate: non vanno ridiscusse a ogni ripresa.
**Come applicare:** prima di riprendere, `git pull` nel vault (Luca può aver modificato note dal telefono), leggere l'indice generale per lo stato e seguire le stesse convenzioni. Collegato a [[progetti-its]].

content.text:
Gli autori stanno scrivendo i moduli 01–07 in background, poi passerà il revisore. Quando hanno finito riprendo da solo: scrivo indice e glossario di AWS, lancio i controlli e faccio il push.

Intanto la repo ha già il primo commit, con l'indice generale e il `.gitignore`. Puoi configurare il telefono e provare a scaricarla:

1. **Crea il token su GitHub**: *Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token*.
   - In *Repository access* scegli *Only select repositories* e poi `Dispense_ITS`.
   - In *Permissions* imposta *Contents* su *Read and write* se vuoi cambiare lo `stato` delle note dal telefono, altrimenti *Read-only*.
2. **Crea un vault vuoto in Obsidian sul telefono**, per esempio "Dispense ITS". Tienilo nella memoria del dispositivo e non in iCloud, per evitare conflitti di sincronizzazione.
3. **Installa il plugin Git**: *Impostazioni → Plugin della community → Attiva → Sfoglia → "Git" → Installa → Abilita*.
4. **Inserisci le credenziali** nelle impostazioni del plugin: come username `ohTara`, come password il token. Il token resta lì, non mandarlo a me.
5. **Scarica la repo**: dalla palette comandi lancia *Git: Clone an existing remote repo* e inserisci `https://github.com/ohTara/Dispense_ITS.git`. Come cartella scegli la radice del vault, poi riavvia Obsidian.
6. **Per gli aggiornamenti** usa *Git: Pull*.

Se compare l'indice generale, il telefono è pronto e la dispensa di AWS arriverà con il prossimo pull.
